note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Several days of acute gastroenteritis-like illness with very loose stools progressing to diarrhea; high fever reported as “seriously hot,” and multiple episodes of vomiting.
  - Possible infectious gastroenteritis; brother has had similar symptoms and classmates reportedly affected.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset about 3 days ago; diarrhoea started watery and became loose; today at least four bowel movements.
  - Vomiting started this morning; last vomiting about two hours ago; unable to keep fluids down.
  - Abdominal pain around the umbilicus, described as sore and non-tolerable to touch; pain comes and goes with urge to toilet.
  - Patient able to urinate; last urination about an hour ago.
- ENT symptoms:
  - No throat swelling/closure, no voice change, no dysphagia/odynophagia, no nasal/ocular symptoms, no stridor or dyspnea reported.
- Past medical history and treatments:
  - No significant prior abdominal problems; otherwise healthy.
  - Brother with similar symptoms; household contact noted.
  - Home remedies: oral rehydration salts (ORS) three times daily for 2 days; ibuprofen for cramps (dose/frequency not documented); vitamins (Vitamin D daily; dose not documented).
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: not documented.
  - Current medications: Oral rehydration salts (dose/route/frequency not documented); ibuprofen (dose/route/frequency not documented) for cramps; Vitamin D daily (dose/frequency not documented).
- Social/contextual:
  - Lives with mother and brother; working from home due to illness; confidentiality confirmed; no accompaniment noted for the visit.

Objective:
- Observable findings:
  - No ENT findings documented.
  - No airway/breathing symptoms noted (no stridor or dyspnea reported).
- Mental status: Not described.
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Other clinical observations: Not described.

Assessment:
- Primary impression: Acute gastroenteritis, likely infectious/viral given familial clustering; risk of dehydration due to vomiting and poor oral intake.
- Rationale: Several days of loose stools with vomiting; fever; household exposure; symptoms ongoing despite oral rehydration attempts.
- Notable facts: No ENT-related manifestations identified; no documented anaphylaxis or allergy-related history.

Plan:
- Immediate actions and guidance:
  - Continue oral rehydration salts with small, frequent sips; avoid overloading stomach to prevent further vomiting.
  - Maintain simple foods (e.g., toast, biscuit); avoid fruit, vegetables, milk if symptoms worsen.
  - Stool sample recommended to evaluate for bacterial infection; aim to test while hydrated; clinic can collect the sample if seen today.
  - Hydration assessment recommended; if unable to keep fluids down, higher risk of dehydration; urgent evaluation advised.
- Instructions to patient/caregiver:
  - Book an urgent clinic appointment to assess hydration and obtain stool sample.
  - If symptoms worsen or patient becomes more unwell, present to emergency department (A&E) promptly.
  - If in clinic: sample can be sent off straightaway; otherwise, sample may need to be mailed (time delay).
  - If you feel more unwell before then: call back to arrange urgent review.
- Escalation criteria / red flags:
  - Inability to keep fluids down, persistent vomiting, reduced urine output, signs of dehydration, fever persists, or worsening abdominal pain.
- Follow-up:
  - Urgent appointment to check hydration status and process stool sample.
  - Post-visit: review results; discuss dehydration management and return precautions.
- COVID-19 vaccine discussion: not addressed.
- Emergency contact instructions (as stated): “If you come into the clinic, you can send that sample off straightaway. Otherwise, we would have to post it out to you which would take time.” “If you’re feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in A and E. So you can call us back in the meantime.” “We can make you an urgent appointment.” “Keep drinking with small sips of rehydration salts.” “If you’re feeling more unwell, you would be seen urgently in A&E.”
